name: Aaron Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Aaron, thanks for doing this. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to tech companies, employers, unions, parties or government. It's confidential, and your name won't be used.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Cool, no worries. I like talking about this stuff, I'm a bit of a nerd about farm tech.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a tractor driver and general hand at Greywater Farms, which is a big farming company, about twelve hundred hectares of wheat, barley and beans, plus fifteen hundred ewes. In autumn I'm drilling seed all day on the big tractor with GPS autosteer, so I mostly watch the screen and do the headland turns. In winter I'm with the shepherds, feeding and moving sheep, and fixing fences. I'm the youngest on the team and I still get the worst jobs, like cleaning out the sprayer.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use AI tools at all?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day, pretty much. I ask the chat app about spray rates and weeds, I use it to plan my budget, and I'm using it to study for my drone pilot licence. Nadia, the farm manager, thinks I'm obsessed. The pay's low though, I rent a flat above the bakery in town and I've got maybe ten days of money in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Huh. That'd be a letdown, honestly. I was hoping for more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decent tool and that's all. I'd still tell the older lads at Greywater to use it for spray plans. Online I'd probably post something like, cool, so we just keep farming then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, for me it doesn't change much. My job's fine, Greywater always needs drivers, but I'm still on low pay with no savings. The one thing I want is to start drone spraying on the side, and that doesn't need AGI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the drone licence by spring and price up a second-hand spraying drone. I'd ask Nadia if Greywater would hire me to do the drone work on their fields. And I'd stop eating out at lunch so I could save a bit toward it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kind of flat, but okay. The worry's money, not the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would a spraying drone cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decent second-hand spraying drone is maybe eight thousand, and I've got about four hundred pounds. So I'd need a loan or someone to go halves. That's the bit that keeps me from just doing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Nadia think of the drone idea?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She laughed the first time, then asked how much it would save on the wet fields where the sprayer gets stuck. Nadia's not against it, she just needs to see the numbers. I'd put them together with the AI and show her.

say: I'd say AI is a **decent tool**, nothing more.
I'd still tell the older lads to use it for **spray plans**.
think: My job's fine because Greywater always **needs drivers**.
The real goal is a **drone spraying** side business, which doesn't need AGI.
do: Ask Nadia to hire me for **drone work** on Greywater fields.
Stop eating out at lunch to **save** toward a drone.
feel: **Flat but okay**, with money the real worry.
S0.quote: A decent second-hand spraying drone is maybe eight thousand, and I've got about four hundred pounds.
fieldNote: Aaron is a **daily AI user** and keen on farm tech.
His constraint is **capital**: an eight-thousand drone on ten days' savings.
He's **unworried about his job**, more about building a side income.

steps.text: Pitch Nadia on paid drone spraying for Greywater's wet fields
Finish the drone pilot licence by spring
Stop buying lunch out and save the money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking tasks first, robots slower. That's sort of what's happening already, to be fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is an opportunity if you're willing to learn. I'd tell people at work the planning will go to AI, so learn the kit. I'd post about my drone stuff and how farm workers can get into tech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I think it's mostly good. My job is hands-on and on the tractor, and Greywater will want someone who understands the new tools. The risk is the office side at Greywater, Nadia's assistant does all the ordering and that'll go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the drone licence and try to get a small loan for a drone, maybe five thousand, and do contract spraying for smaller farms. I'd learn the farm management software properly so I'm useful in planning. I'd keep my job at Greywater while the drone side grows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. A little nervous about the loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nadia's assistant, Jen, who does the ordering and the paperwork. If AI does that, Jen's job shrinks a lot. I'd feel bad, she's been kind to me since I started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A loan on ten days of savings is a big risk. Why take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if I wait to start drone spraying, someone else does it first. I'd start small, one drone, three or four farms. If it doesn't work, I sell the drone and I've lost a bit, not everything.

say: I'd say it's an **opportunity** if you're willing to learn.
I'd tell coworkers the **planning goes to AI**, so learn the kit.
think: My **hands-on tractor job** is safe for now.
**Jen's ordering job** in the office is the one at risk.
do: Take a **five-thousand loan** for a spraying drone.
Keep my **Greywater job** while the drone side grows.
feel: **Excited**, with a little nerve about the loan.
S1.quote: If I wait to start drone spraying, someone else does it first.
fieldNote: Aaron sees **Steady Disruption** as good for his hands-on, tech-friendly role.
He'd take on **debt** for a drone with almost no savings, showing high risk comfort.
He worries about **office colleagues** like Jen more than himself.

steps.text: Borrow five thousand for a second-hand spraying drone
Offer contract drone spraying to three or four small farms
Learn Greywater's farm management software in depth
Keep driving tractors at Greywater full time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028, AGI, and robots by 2031. Okay, that's actually wild.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get ready, it's coming whether you like it or not. I'd tell people to learn the tools now and not wait for the government. I'd probably post a lot about it, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the drone business dies fast, because AGI can plan the spraying and the drones fly themselves. My tractor job lasts till the robots in 2031. So I'd have three years, and I'd need to be on the right side, fixing or running the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd skip the drone loan, because it'd be worthless by 2029. I'd apply for a robotics technician course or an apprenticeship with a machinery dealer straight away. I'd think about moving to a city if that's where the robot jobs are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but excited too. It's like jumping off a high board.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does moving mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leaving town, my mates, the football team on Saturdays. I'd hate leaving, but I can. No kids and no mortgage is the one advantage of being broke and single.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd have three years between AGI and the robots. What's the plan for them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, get into a dealer or robotics course. Years two and three, get hands-on with the first robots coming onto farms. By 2031, I'd want to be the guy who installs them, not the guy who gets replaced.

say: I'd say **get ready**, it's coming either way.
I'd tell people to **learn the tools** now, not wait.
think: The **drone business** dies fast when drones fly themselves.
I'd have **three years** to get on the right side of robots.

fieldNote: Aaron **drops his drone plan** when AGI makes it obsolete.
He'd use the **three-year gap** to retrain as a robot installer.
He sees his **lack of ties** as freedom to move.

steps.text: Apply for a dealer apprenticeship installing farm robots
Leave Greywater for a robotics technician job by 2031
Move to a city if the robot jobs are there

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for AGI, robots in 2034. That's a better runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming, but there's time, so start now. I'd tell my mates to get skills that sit between machines and people. I'd still be the one posting about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The drone business works for a few years, maybe till 2031, then it gets squeezed. My tractor job lasts till about 2034. So I'd have time to make some money, but I'd need to switch before the robots, and I don't know exactly what into.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the drone and run it for three or four years, paying off the loan. Then I'd move into robot servicing with a dealer, using the drone money as a cushion. I'd keep studying with the AI every evening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but with a plan. It's a gamble I'd take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the drone loan isn't paid off by the time AGI arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the risk. I'd try to pay it off in three years by doing more farms. If it isn't, I sell the drone and take the loss. I'd still be young enough to recover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents say about this plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would say get a steady job and stop gambling, and my mum would say do it while you're young. I'd listen to my mum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade, then robots in 2039. That's great for someone my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where everyone gets a fair shot. I'd say get ready but don't panic. I'd tell the older lads it's their kids' problem more than theirs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be forty when the robots come, with a solid trade by then. The drone business could run for years. Honestly, I'm more worried about money in the next two years than the robots in thirteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the drone thing properly, maybe two drones by year five. I'd keep the Greywater job as long as it makes sense. And I'd save, actually save, which I've never done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly good, a bit uneasy about the money side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you've never saved. Why would you now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd have a reason. Buying a second drone, maybe a van. Saving for nothing is hard, but saving for a drone is easy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Jen in the office?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Jen to learn the farm software inside out, because someone has to check the AI. And I'd say it kindly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my drone plan dies and I'd have three years to retrain with no money behind me. What would help is cheap loans for young workers starting a trade, and courses run by the machine dealers that pay you while you learn.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what we're actually good at. Everyone talks about what robots can do, but nobody asks what the farm workers know that the machines don't. I'd like that written down somewhere before it's lost.

headlineQuote: Nobody asks what the farm workers know that the machines don't.
portrait: Aaron is a **27-year-old tractor driver** at Greywater Farms, a large company-run arable and sheep farm.
He uses **AI daily** and wants to start a drone spraying business on the side.
His **risk appetite** is high: he'd borrow for a drone on ten days of savings.
In fast AGI, he'd **drop the drone** and retrain as a robot installer, even moving city.
With more time, his worry is **cash now** rather than robots later.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which kills his drone plan and leaves him three years to retrain.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap loans** for young workers starting a trade.
